doc.title: Jake Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Storyville with Buck Clayton and Jimmy Rushing
summary: The 1959 Storyville gig with Clayton, Rushing, Pee Wee Russell and Bud Freeman, opposite Mulligan's quartet; Sammy Margolis predicts it will change his life.

bands.name: Buck Clayton and Jimmy Rushing group

story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Wow. On the anniversary concert. Oh my. Well I’ve been reading a little bit — Marian McPartland wrote a whole chapter about you.
Yeah. She’s terrific, one of the best people I ever worked with. One of the most enjoyable times in my life.
You told her that in late ‘59 you were playing in Storyville with Buck Clayton and Jimmy Rushing?

Yes. That’s right. That’s right. Jimmy was the singer, Buck, Vic Dickinson, Pee Wee Russell, Bud Freeman. That was the four front line. And Lou Cotto and myself or sometimes George Wein, myself and Champ Jones, who worked for the police department. And the other band was Gerry Mulligan Quartet with Art Farmer played trumpet and Billy Crow and Dave Bailey. You know Dave Bailey wound up being a pilot for F. Lee Bailey, who was a flier himself.
Yeah, he was a pilot for him. He was a Tuskegee Airman, that’s what Dave was.
Was that a particularly significant gig for you?

Yeah, yeah. It was so good I was walking to work one night, I’d been in there with Anita O’Day, I’d been there with the Hi Lo’s, I’d been there with Lambert, Hendricks & Ross, you name it. I was there with these people [inaudible]. I walked in there one night and Sammy Margolis was sitting at the bar and he says, “You playing drums on this job, Jake?” I says, “Yeah, I am, Sammy.” “It’s going to change your life.” I says, “You think so?” He says, “Yeah. It’ll shoot you off in another direction. You’ll never play that corny bebop stuff again.” I says, “You think so?” I says, “Yeah, okay.” I got up and boy was he right. That Buck Clayton was so easy to play with and comfortable and Pee Wee was great, a lot of laughs, and Bud Freeman was there and Vic Dickinson was one of the greatest of all time. It was so easy I didn’t have to do anything. They just played it for us, © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

oh, this is how it’s supposed to go. Everybody’s supposed to contribute. Not like that battling and battling of Maynard, you know, and guys run up and down, trombones and all that, oof, Jesus. Yeah, this was great.
